name: Bolivia
summary_text: Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalized. It has been legal since 1832. The age of consent is 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis, with a three-year close-in-age exemption.  Article 14(II) of the 2009 Constitution prohibits and punishes discrimination based on gender identity.  The Law Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination defines discrimination to include gender identity and defines transphobia. It amended Penal Code article 281 to criminalize gender-identity-based discrimination. Dissemination and incitement to discrimination are punishable by one to five years imprisonment.  Since 2010, Penal Code article 40bis aggravates penalties for crimes motivated by grounds including gender identity.  The Gender Identity Law was passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016, by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May 2016 and took effect on 1 August 2016. It permits persons over 18 to change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service. The procedure is confidential and to be completed within 15 days. It requires a psychological test of voluntary assumption of identity. It does not require sex reassignment surgery. The change is reversible once only.  The first legal gender change under the law was completed on 1 August 2016 by activist Pamela Valenzuela.  The reassigned sex is not recognized for purposes of marriage. In November 2017 the Supreme Court invalidated as unconstitutional a June 2017 Supreme Electoral Tribunal instruction that had directed recognition. An appeal was filed to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018. Article 63 of the Constitution limits marriage to heterosexual couples.  Same-sex couples may register free unions. The Civil Registry recognized such unions in December 2020. A Plurinational Constitutional Court ruling of 22 June 2022 obliging registration took effect on 20 March 2023. Regulations were modified by 21 July 2023 to provide the same requirements and timings as for heterosexual couples. Fifteen couples had registered by January 2023 under Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which had been issued in January 2018.  Legal protection is weakly enforced. The Ombudsman reported that 64 LGBT people were murdered in 2017. Only 14 cases were investigated. None resulted in a sentence.  Societal discrimination against LGBT people is reported as not uncommon. Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people, reported in December 2024, found extensive exclusion.  A 2017 ILGA poll found 64% agreed transgender people should have the same rights, 63% believed they should be protected from employment discrimination and 53% believed they should be allowed to change legal gender.

sources.documents: Requires parties to American Convention to grant same-sex couples access to all family registration including marriage with all derived rights; binding precedent for Bolivian courts used for free union registrations

name: Brunei
summary_text: Brunei maintains a trans-specific offence under the Syariah Penal Code of a man posing as a woman or vice versa. The statute qualifies the conduct by acting without reasonable excuse or for immoral purposes.  A trans visitor cannot align documents with presentation. Brunei does not permit a person to change name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed.  Enforcement is documented. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. A foreign government human rights report for 2017 recorded no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban that year and stated that morality provisions were enforced.  Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in Brunei since 1906 under Straits Settlements law applied through the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated in 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment even if private and consensual.  From 2014 Brunei implemented the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 in stages, with the final stage effective 3 April 2019. The Order bans liwat, defined as anal intercourse between men or between a man and a woman who is not his wife.  The de jure penalty for same-sex relations between men who are married is death by stoning, provided they admit to the acts or four adult male Muslim eyewitnesses testify to the acts. If that evidentiary standard is not met, the maximum penalty is seven years imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping. For unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes.  Sexual relations between women are punishable by any two of three stipulated penalties: caning of forty lashes, a maximum prison term of 10 years, and a fine of up to B$40,000.  Secular law separately criminalizes carnal intercourse against the order of nature. A July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order increased the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years incarceration, primarily applied in cases of rape or child abuse where both attacker and victim are male.  A moratorium on capital punishment affects the de jure stoning penalty. The Sultan stated the moratorium covers the new Shariah code. The government extended it to the Syariah Penal Code Order in May 2019. No execution has been carried out since 1957. A freshness check on 27 September 2026 found the moratorium intact and the 2019 code still in force. The moratorium remains revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning, and the seven-year and whipping penalty operates as the de facto penalty while it continues.  Scope for visitors is not assured. Reporting states the Syariah Penal Code mostly applies to Muslims, who comprise about two-thirds of the population. First-person reporting from April 2019 described a climate of fear with sources speaking anonymously and no assurance of non-enforcement against foreigners.  Protection is not reliable. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public.

sources.title: Syariah Penal Code Order (SPCO)
sources.documents: Core legal status for LGBTQ: de jure death by stoning for liwat between married men if admit or 4 male adult Muslim eyewitnesses testify, otherwise 7 years + 30 strokes whipping; 1 year or 100 lashes for unmarried men; for sex between women combination of 40 lashes caning, up to 10 years prison, up to B$40,000 fine; bans men dressing as women / women as men 'without reasonable excuse' or 'for immoral purposes'
